doc.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013

title: Playing as if no one else is in the rhythm section
summary: The bassist as illusionist, hearing the sound of a song rather than chord symbols, and learning harmony by ear.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: That’s great. I saw a thing that you said which really caught my eye. And it went something like, “Assume there’s nobody else, tell students to play as if there’s no one else in the rhythm section.” And the first time I went like “wow.” Some people would say, like what do you mean, the rhythm section has to be one, everybody has to be together. But then you went on to explain it. I wish you would explain it again, because I found it really very interesting.

Well bass players, I think we have, I assume you’re the only harmonic and rhythmic substance that there is. In other words, don’t — if the piano player’s not there, does that mean you can’t play? If the drummer’s not there, does that mean you can’t play with good time? So you don’t really need them. And they don’t need you either. If they play with good time and good sense of harmony and everything, that’s how solo pianists can — I mean the piano is an orchestra, so I mean they can do a lot more things obviously, than with the bass. But the bass can actually do something alone and make people believe they’re hearing harmony if they sculpt and craft their bass lines. And they can — I call the bassist — we have to be illusionists, a magician. We have to make people hear and see things that aren’t there, and not miss them. Now that’s quite a chore, and yet it’s not as difficult as one might think. But I mean Bach would have been a fantastic jazz musician. Because he was improvising. But let’s say the Bach Cello Suites. There’s no harmony. There’s no chords. I mean once in a while you might have some fifths and stuff like this, but it’s about placement and resolution, and how he connects things. And you hear harmony everywhere. And so rhythm changes has a sound, blues has a sound, “My One and Only Love” has a sound. Any song has its own sound. And if you can get that sound, not play the changes — people play the changes, it’s the formula that kind of gets you into it. And I learned — I didn’t know what all the hieroglyphics of sharp fives and plus zeros — that was hieroglyphics to me. I knew the big letters, but it had a sound. And my ears said, “Eww that didn’t sound right,” so I moved my hand to another note. And it was generally a half-step above or below. And that’s how I edited myself. And eventually I learned why I liked the sound. And now I can put something on this sound, a symbol, and now I know.
You sort of played it first by trial and error, then learned why it sounded good?

Right. And then tried to be consistent with that. Because I had a lot of great on-the-job training as a bassist. I listened to a lot of records and I would sing along with them and play, but I didn’t know harmony for a long time.
